questions.question: What is the Divine Right of Kings and how does it affect "Macbeth"?
questions.correctAnswer: Divine Right of Kings meant monarchs were appointed by God. Killing a king was a sin against divine order. In "Macbeth," regicide triggers chaos in nature and leads to Macbeth's downfall, reinforcing this belief.

questions.question: Why did Shakespeare include witches in "Macbeth"?
questions.correctAnswer: James I was obsessed with witchcraft and wrote a book about identifying witches. Including witches appealed to James, established the play's evil atmosphere, and reflected genuine Jacobean fears.

questions.question: How did the Globe Theatre shape Shakespeare's writing?
questions.correctAnswer: The Globe had no sets or artificial lighting, so Shakespeare used language to create setting and atmosphere. The thrust stage meant audience surrounded actors, creating intimacy. All-male casts meant boys played women.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response 25 marks: "How does Shakespeare use Jacobean context to create meaning in the opening scenes of Macbeth?" <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Shakespeare's opening scenes are steeped in Jacobean anxiety, exploiting the cultural and political fears of 1606 to establish the play's atmosphere of moral chaos. The witches' declaration "Fair is foul, and foul is fair" inverts moral categories entirely — for an audience conditioned by James I's Protestant theology to see witchcraft as demonic agency, these figures represent genuine evil, not theatrical spectacle. Their paradoxical language establishes a world where moral absolutes have collapsed, prefiguring Macbeth's own moral disorientation. When Duncan arrives at Macbeth's castle and praises its "pleasant seat," the dramatic irony operates on both textual and contextual levels: the audience knows Macbeth plans murder, but for a Jacobean audience who believed in the Divine Right of Kings, Duncan's trust makes the coming regicide not merely criminal but sacrilegious — a violation of God's appointed order. Lady Macbeth's invocation "unsex me here" directly contravenes Jacobean gender ideology, which insisted on feminine submission and domesticity; her rejection of femininity to embrace cruelty would have been read as further evidence of the supernatural's corrupting influence. Shakespeare thus embeds Jacobean anxieties about witchcraft, kingship, and gender into the very fabric of his opening, ensuring that the play's horror resonates with the real fears of his original audience.
